The applied voltage was also used to keep the CNTs off adsorbing on the gate electrode. A CNT-based planar-gate-type electron source panel was successfully fabricated with the special electrophoretic process. In addition, the field emission characteristics of the planar-gate-type electron source panel were also studied.

The commercial CNTs were synthesized by CVD method. First, these raw CNTs were purified and shorted by refluxing in mixture of concentrated sulfuric and nitric acids (3:1; 98% and 70%, respectively) for 6 h at 60 °C. Then, the CNTs were washed with water and dried in air at 120 °C for 12 h. Thirdly, the processed CNTs were dispersed in isopropyl alcohol solution that had contained a little-dissolved $\mathrm{Mg(NO_{3})_{2}\cdot6H_{2}O}$ . A little amount of dissolved ethyl cellulose was added to the suspension to disperse the CNTs. The CNTs suspension was ultrasonically dispersed for about a day, and then centrifuged for 20 min at 3000 rpm in order to remove the large-sized CNTs conglomerations. The top fraction of the suspension was used in the electrophoresis procedures.

The whole manufacture process of the planar-gate-type electron source panel was illustrated in Fig. 1. The indium tin oxide (ITO)-coated glass was cleaned in acetone for 10 min under ultrasonication. After rinsing the ITO by alcohol and deionized water, the ITO-coated glass was baked in a furnace at 60 °C for 20 min. Next, the substrate was coated by photoresist layer using spin coating method, and then, a photoresist pattern was formed by conventional photolithographic technology. Etching of the ITO layer on glass was carried out in an ITO etchant (mixture
of hydrochloric acid and zinc powder). After ITO etching, the photoresist pattern was removed using acetone. Then, an interdigitated electrode of ITO was obtained as substrate for assembling CNTs. One of the two groups of interdigitated electrodes was used as cathode stripe for CNTs and the other one was used as the gate stripe, respectively. In final step, the processed substrate was immersed in the CNTs suspension and a direct current (DC) voltage of 30 V was applied between the two groups of interdigitated electrodes for 3 min. The CNTs were assembled only on cathode stripes. Then the planar-gate-type electron source panel was obtained.

To study the field emission characteristics of the planar-gate-type electron source panel, the sample was brought into the vacuum chamber, where the base pressure was $9 \times 10^{-5}$ Pa. A quartz spacer of 500 $\mu$ m thickness was placed on the substrate to isolate the cathode from the anode.

Fig. 2 shows a typical image of the planar-gate-type electron source panel, observed by the optical microscopy. The cathode stripes and the gate stripes were interdigitated and paralleled on the same plane. The cathode stripe width, gate stripe width and the distance between gate and cathode were same, that is about $25 \mu m$ . The CNTs were selectively assembled on cathode stripes and the each cathode stripe has the same packing density. The CNTs were not adsorbed on the gate electrodes. In Fig. 2, inset is the cross-section scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of CNTs. It clearly shows the morphology of CNTs. The CNTs are randomly oriented. Many CNTs vertically protrude the cathode stripe.

electrodes, the schematic electric field, shown in Fig. 3, would occur around substrate.
To understand what happens next, imagine the substrate as a stage where a specific electrical "landscape" is set up.
The substrate was immersed in the suspension and the CNTs migrated towards the cathode stripes instead of the positive one under the electric field.

You might wonder: why would carbon nanotubes (CNTs) move toward the negative electrode (cathode) rather than the positive one (anode)? This behavior is counter-intuitive if you assume the CNTs are neutral. The key lies in their surface chemistry.
This was because the $Mg^{2+}$ ions were absorbable by suspending CNTs, and then the double electron layers around the CNTs in the suspension formed [12].

Let's break down this mechanism. The $Mg^{2+}$ ions in the solution attach to the surface of the CNTs. This attachment effectively gives the CNTs a net positive charge. In electrostatics, opposite charges attract. Therefore, the positively charged CNTs are drawn toward the negatively charged cathode stripes. This process creates what is known as an electrical double layer around each CNT, a fundamental concept in colloid science that governs how particles interact in a fluid under an electric field.

Once the CNTs reach the target, they don't just sit loosely; they bond firmly.
The CNTs adhered strongly on the cathode stripes. The good adhesion was attributed to from formation of metal hydroxide, which assists the interfacial bonding ([12], [13]).

Think of this metal hydroxide as a chemical "glue" that forms at the interface between the CNT and the electrode, ensuring a robust connection that is critical for reliable electron emission later on.

Simultaneously, the system is designed with precision to prevent unwanted deposition.
At the same time, the gate positive voltage can keep CNTs off adsorbing on the gate
stripes. The gate stripes are positively charged, which repels the positively charged CNTs, ensuring they only settle on the cathode
stripes. Moreover, the electric field was same around each cathode stripe, which will lead that each cathode stripe has the same packing density.
This uniformity is a major advantage. Because the electric field distribution is consistent across the device, the density of CNTs on each stripe is identical.
Therefore, the process could be applied to fabrication of large area electron source.
This scalability is vital for practical applications, as it ensures that a large panel will perform uniformly, rather than having "hot spots" or weak areas.
Field emission characteristics of the planar-gate-type electron source panel were measured with triode mode.

Now that we have fabricated the device, we need to test how well it works. The term "triode mode" refers to a three-electrode configuration: a cathode (emitter), an anode (collector), and a gate (control electrode). This setup allows for precise control over the electron flow, much like a valve controlling water flow.
In measurements, the applied anode bias was fixed at less than 1400 V to avoid diode-type electron emission.

Why this specific limit? If the voltage between the anode and cathode is too high, electrons might be pulled directly from the cathode to the anode without the help of the gate, bypassing the control mechanism. By keeping the anode bias below this threshold, we ensure that the gate voltage is the primary driver of emission.
The measurement results were shown in Fig. 4. It indicated that the emission current could be controlled effectively by the gate
This is the core function of the device: using a low-voltage gate signal to modulate a high-current electron beam.

Fig. 4(a) shows field emission characteristics of the electron source with different anode bias. The anode currents increase with higher anode biases under the same gate voltages. This could be understood by a coupling of anode biases to gate voltages to enhance electrons emission. That suggested a triode mode of operation in this structure.

we are observing a synergistic effect. The anode bias doesn't just collect electrons; it also influences the electric field at the cathode surface. A higher anode voltage strengthens the field, making it easier for electrons to tunnel out of the CNTs (a quantum mechanical process known as field emission). This "coupling" confirms that the device is operating in a true triode mode, where both the gate and anode voltages play active roles in determining the emission current.

The anode bias was fixed at the value, which just avoided the electron emission in the diode-like structure. Then, the emission current from the nanotubes was turned on and modified by increasing gate voltage.
This experimental setup isolates the effect of the gate voltage. By holding the anode bias constant at a safe level, any change in current can be directly attributed to the gate's influence.
Fig. 4(b) shows field emission characteristics of the planar-gate-type electron source panel with different geometry structure parameter.
Next, we investigate how the physical dimensions of the device affect its performance.

When geometry structure parameter $W$ (the cathode stripe width, gate stripe width and the distance between gate stripe and cathode stripe) was changed from 50 to $25\mu \mathrm{m}$ , the anode currents increased under same gate voltages and same anode bias. It was caused by the decrease of $W$ , which enhanced the surface electric field of CNTs.

This is a crucial insight into device design. The parameter $W$ represents the characteristic length scale of the electrode geometry. In electrostatics, electric fields are strongest where the distance between conductors is smallest or where the curvature of the conductor is high. By reducing $W$ from 50 micrometers to 25 micrometers, we are effectively tightening the geometry. This concentration of electric field lines at the CNT tips significantly enhances the local surface electric field. Since field emission current is exponentially sensitive to the electric field strength, even a modest increase in field leads to a substantial increase in current.
In order to obtain higher current density at the same gate voltage, the decrease of $W$ was needed.
This tells us that miniaturizing the electrode features is a powerful strategy for boosting emission efficiency.

In our experiment, the optimal emission characteristic showed that the current densities could be modified from 0 to $216\mu \mathrm{A/cm}^2$ by increasing the gate voltages from 0 to $150\mathrm{V}$ with anode bias of $1400\mathrm{V}$ for $W$ was $25\mu \mathrm{m}$ and anode-cathode spacing was $500\mu \mathrm{m}$ .

These numbers provide a concrete benchmark for the device's performance. A current density of $216 \mu \mathrm{A/cm}^2$ is a significant value for a planar emitter, indicating that the CNTs are emitting electrons efficiently. The fact that this is achieved with a gate voltage of only 150 V demonstrates the low power consumption of the control mechanism.

An emission stability of the planar-gate-type electron source panel was measured at constant gate voltage and constant anode voltage for initial emission current density of $200 \mu A/cm^{2}$ for 60 min.
Performance is not just about how much current you can get, but how stable that current is over time. A flickering or degrading electron source is useless for most applications.
The current variation was shown in Fig. 5 as a function of time. The electron source exhibited stable electron emission without degradation. The emission current fluctuation was less than 7.5%.
A fluctuation of less than 7.5% over an hour is a strong indicator of reliability.
The good stability of field emission (FE) current density with respect to time may be attributed to the CNTs, which adhered strongly on the cathode stripes.

Recall the metal hydroxide bonding we discussed earlier? That strong adhesion prevents the CNTs from being ripped away by the electric field or from shifting position, which would cause current fluctuations.
The emission stability also prefigured that the planar-gate-type electron source panel has repeatability of electron emission performance and long lifetime.
This stability suggests that the device can be turned on and off repeatedly without losing performance, a key requirement for practical electronic devices.
